title: Experimental designs
examples: When should I use a repeated measures design instead of an independent measures design?
What are the main advantages and disadvantages of using matched pairs?
Can I mix these designs, or do I have to choose just one?

explain.say: Today we are looking at experimental designs in psychology. These designs help us test cause and effect. We will learn about three main types of designs.

First we look at independent measures designs. In this design, different groups of people are used. Each group experiences a different condition in the study. For example, one group might use a new learning method. A separate group would use the old method.

Next we consider repeated measures designs. Here, the same group of participants is tested multiple times. They go through every condition in the experiment. For instance, you could test memory before and after reading. The same people take both tests.

The third design is matched pairs. This design pairs participants based on a similar characteristic. Both members of a pair experience both conditions. For example, you could test twins on two different tasks. Their similar genetics help control for differences.

In a real-life study, imagine testing a new drug for anxiety. You could use a repeated measures design. You test the same people before taking the drug and again after a month. This shows individual change over time.

draw.text: Real Life: Drug Testing Over Time

explain.say: A common mistake is assuming that because a group is small, the design is perfect. Remember that every design has limitations. For instance, repeated measures can suffer from practice effects. This means people get better just by taking the test repeatedly.

items: Solution: Include a control group if possible

faq.q: What is the main difference between independent and repeated measures?
faq.a: In independent measures, different people are in different groups. In repeated measures, the same people are tested in every group.
asks: Does the same person take all the tests?
What is the difference between using separate groups and using the same group?

faq.q: When are matched pairs best to use?
faq.a: Matched pairs are useful when you need to control for pre-existing individual differences. This is especially true when studying related individuals, like siblings.
asks: Should I use matched pairs for twins?
What is the benefit of matching subjects?

faq.q: Can I use a design that controls for both practice and individual differences?
faq.a: Yes, a combination design might be appropriate. You could use a mixed design, which combines elements of both types.
asks: Is there a mix of designs?

faq.q: What is the main threat to internal validity in these designs?
faq.a: The main threat is often history or maturation. History refers to an outside event affecting the results. Maturation refers to natural changes in the participants over time.
asks: What is the biggest threat to the study's reliability?

faq.q: Does the sample size matter for all designs?
faq.a: Yes, a larger sample size generally increases the statistical power of your findings. However, the design choice dictates how that sample is used.
asks: Do I need many people for this?
How big should my sample be?

facts: Independent measures designs require separate groups for each condition.
Repeated measures designs test the same participants multiple times.
Matched pairs control for individual differences by pairing similar subjects.
A major threat to internal validity is the history effect.

quiz.say: A researcher tests students' reaction times using a new study technique and an old study technique. They use two completely different groups of students for each technique.
quiz.why: This design uses two separate groups to test two different conditions.

wrong.0: This would mean the same students took both tests, which is not the case here.
wrong.1: This requires pairing subjects based on similarity, which was not mentioned.
wrong.2: This design is more complex and involves combining multiple types of testing.

quiz.say: A psychologist studies the effect of caffeine on mood by testing the same group of participants before and after they consume caffeine.
quiz.why: Because the same group is tested at two different times, it is a repeated measures design.

wrong.0: This design aims to show relationships, not cause and effect through manipulation.
wrong.2: Independent measures require different groups for each condition.
wrong.3: Matched pairs are used when you need to pair up similar individuals.
